assumptions.summary: Water is treated as stable, incompressible, viscous, and Boussinesq with restricted density variation.
Occupant agitation is assumed to make temperature instantaneously uniform, body heat is ignored, and water convection is removed.
BWP tub walls are steady, BWOP walls/bottom are adiabatic, and only full-bath states are considered.

contributions.summary: Derives an equivalent hot-water-tube surrogate and then restores real faucet/overflow geometry in ANSYS.
Pairs spatial isotherms with volume-average, extrema, and surface/tub heat-loss statistics.
Uses occupied spatial evidence and agitation behavior to motivate a lumped uniform-temperature model.
Defines water, comfort, operation frequency, and difficulty before comparing CI and DCI.
Carries two schedules through a four-criterion distance-to-ideal ranking.
Changes only the water-surface interface and reruns natural cooling.
Converts model outcomes into preference-specific operating and safety advice.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Tables define thermal constants, geometry, temperatures, flows, heat quantities, and model abbreviations.
Nominal tub volume is 0.3 m3 with 0.4 m height, 1.4 by 0.7 m top, and 1.0 by 0.5 m bottom.
The paper fixes 313 K desired water, 318 K inflow, and a 40-minute cleansing horizon.
Five-point input, environment, geometry, material, and occupant scenarios feed tables and response curves.

edges.handoff: The water-air coefficient and boundary condition enter the BWOP field solve.
The equivalent-tube derivation supplies an analytical heating boundary before ANSYS restores the real faucet/overflow geometry.
The unoccupied spatial field provides geometry and baseline behavior for the stationary-person field.
The motion argument reduces the occupied spatial field to a uniform temperature used by the lumped loss model.
The same water-air coefficient becomes the dominant BWP loss term.
Total lumped loss Qd enters the continuous-flow energy recurrence.
Total lumped loss Qd enters the heating and cooling phases of DCI.
CI water, comfort, complexity, and difficulty scores form one FCE alternative.
DCI threshold results and scores form the competing FCE alternative.
The bubble scenario retains BWP and replaces only the water-surface loss interface.

feedbacks: Sensitivity returns operating and geometry factors to BWOP/BWP outputs.
The bubble scenario returns an altered surface loss to BWP natural cooling.
The Appendix returns CI/DCI and spatial safety conclusions to the user.

independent_extensions.summary: Rebuild the CFD model with complete buoyancy closure, inlet/outlet boundaries, mesh independence, residual tolerances, and archived solver state.
Measure occupant mixing and body heat transfer, then validate the spatial-to-lumped reduction by timescale separation.
Reconstruct criteria with consistent directions, elicited weights, and preference/weight sensitivity before ranking CI/DCI.
Measure bubble thickness, porosity, conductivity, evaporation, and decay, then test against physical cooling data.
Convert the user appendix into sensor-based thresholds, safe flow bounds, and explicit fallback instructions.

models.section: Water-air natural convection and surface loss
models.summary: Film temperature and Gr/Ra/Nu correlations produce the air-side coefficient; convective and radiative surface terms define the BWOP/BWP free-surface boundary.
An equivalent tube combines outside convection, tube conduction, inside forced convection, and a mean driving temperature; this is an analytical surrogate, not the final ANSYS geometry.

Continuity, momentum, and energy equations with free-surface and adiabatic boundaries are handed to ANSYS FLUENT using the real faucet and overflow geometry; isotherms and volume statistics are returned.
ANSYS fields with a stationary person show nonuniform water and body-surface temperatures; the paper argues that discomfort causes agitation and then assumes instantaneous uniform mixing for BWP.
The uniform BWP state loses heat through the water surface and through a steady tub-wall/tub-air series path; MATLAB combines Q1 and Q2 into the natural-cooling curve used by both control schedules.
At fixed bath volume, inflow equals overflow and the mixed outlet follows the next water state; a discrete energy balance produces the CI curve, water volume, comfort proxy, and operation indices.
The faucet opens at 312 K, heats to 314 K, then closes for natural cooling; alternating energy balances produce a sawtooth trajectory and lower reported water use.

Water, inverse-variance comfort, operation complexity, and operative difficulty are normalized against an ideal allocation, weighted, and reduced to a scalar distance; the paper reports DCI 0.1404 versus CI 0.3624.
The BWP water-surface interface is replaced by one-dimensional conduction through a porous bubble layer; varying effective conductivity changes the natural-cooling curve.

results_trace.summary: Reported field statistics are 313.1946 K average, 318.0238 K maximum, and 312.9532 K minimum.
CI reports 0.0735 m3 added water and inverse-deviation comfort 10.6021.
DCI uses 312/314 K thresholds and reports 0.0524 m3 water and comfort 1.67757.
The paper selects DCI from reported distances 0.1404 versus 0.3624 for CI.
The paper ranks water volume above area, material, and occupant-volume effects.
Lower effective bubble conductivity produces slower reported cooling.
Continuous calibration and threshold-by-feel are offered as two user branches with mixing/scald notes.

limitations: All 44 pages were rendered and reviewed through six contact sheets; the formula, CFD, result, sensitivity, bubble, and user-advice pages were inspected at full resolution.
OCR damages mathematical glyphs, so rendered equations, tables, axes, and units are authoritative.
The PDF metadata title is unrelated to the bathtub paper and the Abstract prints January 28, 2014; paper identity follows the manifest path, filename, summary sheet, and content.
Raw ANSYS/MATLAB projects, empirical data, convergence logs, criterion calibration, and uncertainty propagation are absent.

Represent unoccupied and occupied baths, including person motion.
Choose a water-saving, comfortable, safe hot-water strategy.
Test geometry, inflow, environment, material, and occupant changes.
Extend the model to a bubble bath additive and explain operation to users.

title: Bathtub Temperature and Inflow Strategy
unresolved_questions: Which viscosity exponents, heat units, and Q definitions make the thermal network dimensionally consistent?
What mesh, buoyancy model, turbulence setting, inlet/outlet boundary, residual tolerance, and grid study reproduce the ANSYS fields?
What mixing time and body heat flux justify replacing occupied spatial fields by an instant uniform state?
Are all plotted time axes seconds rather than minutes, and how do the 40-minute horizon and 94-minute DCI period reconcile?
What faucet area and flow units reproduce 73.5 L and 52.4 L?
How should comfort, operation complexity, and difficulty be oriented, normalized, calibrated, and weighted?
Can the reported FCE matrix and DCI ranking be reproduced from reconciled raw criteria?
How do coupled geometry factors, bubble properties, uncertainty, and real bath measurements change the recommendation?

verification.summary: Isotherms and Table 4 jointly report spatial pattern and aggregate field statistics.
Component and total cooling curves expose the reported dominance of water-air loss.
Trajectory, water amount, temperature deviation, and operation criteria are reported together.
Threshold trajectory, water amount, deviation, period, and difficulty are reported together.
Raw criteria and final FCE values are shown, though the normalization is not independently reproducible.
Tables and curves provide internal scenario checks, not external validation.

weaknesses.summary: Viscosity powers and units appear inconsistent.
Boussinesq coupling and boundary conditions are incomplete.
Mesh, solver, turbulence, residual, and convergence settings are missing.
Flux units, sign, and Kelvin/Celsius conversion conflict.
Instant mixing, no convection, and no body heat are mutually weak assumptions.
Time axes, 40-minute horizon, and 94-minute operation period conflict.
Raw value, normalization matrix, and weight derivation are not reproducible.
Several scenarios change coupled factors and cannot isolate one sensitivity.
Layer thickness, properties, porosity, lifetime, evaporation, and experiment are absent.
Numeric thresholds and reproducible faucet settings are not carried into the advice.

writing_logic.summary: Identify the classified task before any model claim. | Name {problem class} and keep all later claims inside its source boundary.
Open with the paired occupancy models and the control-decision route. | Introduce {case models}, then {control alternatives}, then {decision method}.
Restate the state variable, constant-temperature goal, and water-use constraint. | Model {state} in {space/time}; keep it near {target} without excessive {resource}.
Declare the fluid regime before equations. | Treat {fluid} as {regime}; omit {small effect} within {scope}.
Place constants, variables, units, and model abbreviations before derivation. | Define {constants and variables} with {units}, then introduce {model abbreviations}.
Make the unoccupied spatial model the base for the occupied model. | Begin with {base case}, produce {field output}, then hand it to {later case}.
Open the occupied model by explicitly inheriting the unoccupied analysis. | After {prior case}, consider {new case} and retain {shared components}.
Name continuous and threshold schedules before defining decision criteria. | Feed {loss model} into {continuous and event-triggered schedules}, then define {criteria}.
Translate CFD field and volume statistics into spatial mechanism and safety claims. | Use {field and statistics} to locate {cold/hot regions}, explain {mechanism}, and bound {safety claim}.
Declare outputs before varying operating and environment inputs. | Hold {baseline}; vary {input}; record {field, heat-flux, and temperature metrics}.
Connect spatial solver capability to field visualization and volume statistics. | Retain {solver capability} because it produces {field evidence and statistics} for {decision use}.
Translate the model comparison into two user preference branches. | If {preference}, choose {strategy}; perform {steps}; monitor {state}.
Close provenance without creating new reusable argument evidence. | Cite {source} for {law, constant, solver, or method} and preserve its evidence boundary.
